newsitem.title: JAPAN: Poisoning scare cuts Japan beef imports.
newsitem.headline: Poisoning scare cuts Japan beef imports.

text.p: Japanese consumers are still shunning imported beef and cattle organs after this summer's outbreak of the deadly O-157 germ, which has been blamed on several sources, including meat products, traders say.
"Beef consumption in Japan, particularly of beef organs and raw calves' liver, has remained weak since the outbreak of the germ," a trader at a major trading house said on Tuesday.
He said many retailers stopped selling cattle organs, or have reduced the shelf space allocated to imported beef while allowing more space for domestic beef and other meats.
He said the situation was likely to continue for the foreseeable future, amid perceptions among consumers that imported beef was more dangerous than domestic beef.
Officials this summer found the O-157 colon bacillus in some imported foodstuffs, including beef intestine.
None of the products had been distributed and officials still do not know the actual source and transmission routes of this summer's epidemic, which killed 11 and made more than 9,500 ill.
Two weeks ago, students and teachers at an elementary school 600 km (360 miles) north of Tokyo were infected with the O-157 germ.
Traders doubted this latest outbreak would further depress Japan's meat consumption, but expected it would make a recovery in beef sales all the more difficult.
Japan's beef imports plunged 29.5 percent in August from the same month last year, and one trader predicted beef imports for the whole year would fall by around 10 percent.

Inventories of imported beef also surged 44.7 percent in August to 136,453 tonnes, from August last year, although this was off a modest 3.1 percent from record high inventories in July, according to the Livestock Industry Promotion Corp.

An official at the industry body said July's inventory surge was an aberration, as traders imported large amounts of beef ahead of an August 1 increase in frozen beef tariffs to 50 percent from 46.2 percent.
But traders said the weak beef sales also contributed to the jump in inventories, as importers were forced to freeze some of their refrigerated beef imports due to slack demand.

"I think it will take three to six months for the rising stocks to be worked off," one trader said, adding inventory falls would hinge on sales of beef for shabu-shabu, a popular winter stew of thinly sliced beef and vegetables cooked in boiling water.
Wholesale import beef prices have been battered by the oversupply with prices of U.S. chuck ribs to large-lot end-users falling nearly 40 percent from the same period a year ago.
